title: queueing-phase-diagram-exploration-scratch-lina
content:
Scratchpad: Queueing phase diagram exploration
Owner: Lina Hart (personal notes)
Dates: experiments 2024-11-03 -> 2024-11-17
Context / motivation:
- Trying to build an intuitive phase diagram for our inference runtime: map arrival rate (lambda) vs observed queue depth and tail latency under different cache/warmup regimes.
- Goal: identify the ‘knee’ where queueing transitions from bounded to runaway, and correlate with warm-cache hit rate and batching behavior.
- Quick use-case: decide autoscaling policy thresholds and whether to trigger graceful degradation (smaller model variant) when in the unstable region.

Environment / config:
- Runtime: serving-runtime @ commit c8f9a6 (batching/backpressure changes merged)
- Hardware: 4x A100-40GB, 16 CPU cores per worker, driver pool with 3 workers, network intra-rack
- Model: open-llama-13b quantized int8 (KV cache enabled)
- Request type: single-turn text completion, prompt tokens ~120, generation limit 128 (avg tokens per request 40)
- Latency SLO target: p99 < 250ms for host-tier workloads
- Batching: dynamic adaptive batching enabled (max batch 64, max delay 20ms)
- Cache: two modes tested: warm-cache (primed with 10k recent prefixes) vs cold-cache (cache disabled)

Traffic shapes used:
1) steady Poisson arrivals (baseline)
2) controlled ramp: 50 -> 800 qps over 10 minutes
3) single microburst: base 80 qps, 5s spike to 900 qps
4) sawtooth: 60s low / 30s high repeating

Key derived numbers (observed service rate mu estimates):
- Measured sustainable throughput per GPU (no queue, high hit-rate): ~220 qps (steady-state measurement)
- Hence mu_total (3 workers * 220) ~ 660 qps theoretical
- Observed knee around lambda_total approx 620-660 qps depending on cache hits
- Utilization rho = lambda / mu approximations used to reason about stability

Representative runs (summaries):
Run A (warm-cache, ramp):
- Ramp to 650 qps, held 5 min. p50 45ms, p90 102ms, p99 262ms -> slight breach at tail.
- Queue depth stabilized around 18-26 items per worker. Batching increased effective throughput but added 10-30ms batching delay.
- Observation: warm-cache absorbed up to ~620 qps with p99 ~240-260ms; above 640 saw sharp growth in queue depth.

Run B (cold-cache, ramp):
- Same ramp to 650 qps. p50 78ms, p90 210ms, p99 560ms -> large tail; CPU async overhead for KV misses visible.
- Queue depth grew steadily; system entered backpressure and shedding behaviors at ~700 qps.
- Note: model cold KVs doubled average decode time per token in these runs.

Run C (microburst 5s to 900 qps, warm-cache):
- Immediate p99 spike to 1.2s during burst; after 12s queue depths stayed elevated and decay took ~45s.
- Adaptive batching aggregated many arrivals during burst, creating transient big batches -> improved throughput but worsened tail latency.

Simple ASCII phase diagram sketch (arrival rate on x, queue depth / unstable region on y):

  queue  |        unstable region (runaway)         
  depth  |           /\                            
         |          /  \                          
         |         /    \   bounded region         
         |--------/------\------------------------
         |       /        \                       
         |      /          \                      
         +------------------------------------------
            0   200  400  600  800  1000  (qps)

Interpretation notes:
- Two-parameter sensitivity: cache-hit-rate and batch-delay cap matter most. With high hit-rate, mu effectively increases (less token decode work), moving the knee right.
- Adaptive batching reduces average cost-per-request but increases variance; this shifts the p50-p90 down, but p99 can worsen under bursts because batches coalesce and decode time scales superlinearly with batch size for some kernels.
- Short microbursts cause persistent queue inflation because our backpressure has hysteresis (we only shed or scale after thresholds sustained for multiple seconds).

Quantitative check (simple M/M/3-ish intuition):
- If mu_gpu ~220 qps, 3 workers => mu=660; for lambda=640, rho ~ 0.97 -> system is critically loaded, small variance leads to long queues. This matches observed knee around 620-660 qps.
- Cold-cache effectively lowers mu (observed ~180 per GPU), pushing knee to ~540 qps.

Quick heuristics to operationalize:
- Autoscale trigger: target scale-up when sustained 1min avg qps > 0.85 * mu_total (current config). For our setup ~0.85*660 ~ 561 qps.
- Burst protection: enable short-term soft-shed for burst durations < 10s (respond with 429 upstream) rather than letting queue inflate; faster user-facing failure preferable to 1s+ p99s.
- Batch delay cap: reduce max batching delay to 10ms for critical low-latency tiers to reduce p99 under burst (tradeoff: throughput loss ~8-12%).
- Cache priming: maintain warm-cache for top-heavy customers; missing KVs add nonlinear tail.

Notable surprising findings:
- Batch-size vs decode-time: beyond batch size ~40, decode time growth is superlinear on the quantized path (likely kernel-level memory pressure). Large bursts that create batch sizes >40 cause disproportionate p99s.
- Slow decay: after a burst, queue depth sometimes takes multiple minutes to return if concurrent background maintenance (checkpoint upload) hits same worker. Park checkpoints to low-traffic windows.

Plots I sketched locally (referenced in linked_artifacts):
- phase-diagram-11-07.png (scatter: arrival rate vs avg queue depth)
- runC-burst-latency-heatmap.png (per-worker latency over time)

Actionable next steps / experiments:
1) Run controlled microburst sweep varying batch-delay cap {5ms,10ms,20ms} and max-batch {16,32,64} to quantify p99 tradeoffs. (priority)
2) Simulate a small global change: if we limit batch size to 32, what throughput lost at 99th percentile under steady high load?
3) Try speculative early-respond for low-confidence long-tail tokens (i.e., cut generation when per-token decode time exceeds threshold) — see JIRA-INF-981 for proposal.
4) Short-term: implement soft-shed (<10s) and measure user-visible error fraction vs tail-latency reduction.

Quick TODOs / notes to self:
- Share this with Omar + SRE tomorrow; gather their thoughts on soft-shed UX.
- Add a column in telemetry to tag batch-size at request level so we can correlate p99 with batch-size distribution (current tracing lacks this granularity).
- Check PR #1423 for kernel-time profiling toggles; enable for next runs.

References / offline reading:
- Kleinrock queueing theory notes (chapter on multi-server critical regime) — refresh intuition.
- Kernel mem pressure issues: internal perf thread notes (Confluence-4462).

One-line summary for a quick Slack update:
- Found a sharp knee around 620-660 qps (warm vs cold cache shifts it); bursts create big batches that amplify p99s — short-term mitigation: tighten batch-delay and add soft-shed for brief spikes.

End of scratchpad.
